problems.stem: A policy memo says: "All students will use the AI writing coach for the persuasive essay unit." Why is a low-tech fallback needed?
options: Because the AI coach is too expensive.
Because the memo makes the tool a single point of failure: if it is down, consent is declined, or a device fails, learning stops.
Because the unit should not include persuasion.
problems.explanation: A defensible memo names a fallback so the AI tool is never the only path to the learning target.

problems.stem: The memo says nothing about families who decline AI use. What problem does this silence create?
options: It makes the AI tool mandatory by omission, since declining families are left with no equivalent path.
It is fine because most families agree.
It means the unit cannot be graded.
problems.explanation: Without a stated opt-out and an equivalent route, the tool becomes required by default for everyone.

problems.stem: Which arrangement best protects students without reliable home devices while still allowing AI use?
options: Assign the AI coach as nightly homework for everyone.
Keep all AI use in class on school devices, never as required homework, with a printed peer-review fallback for opted-out students.
Tell students to use a library if they have no device.
Drop the unit for students without devices.
problems.explanation: In-class use on school devices plus a non-AI path keeps home access from becoming a penalty.

problems.stem: A reviewer asks what happens to student essays the AI coach processes. Which memo line answers the privacy check?
options: The tool is popular with teachers.
The vendor contract bars retention of student text for model training.
Students should avoid writing anything personal.
problems.explanation: Stating the data-retention boundary answers the privacy check a reviewer would raise.
